verses.zh: 「人子啊，你要拿一块砖，摆在你面前，将一座耶路撒冷城画在其上，
verses.en: “And you, son of man, take a brick[NOTE:1] and set it in front of you. Inscribe[NOTE:2] a city on it—Jerusalem.
notes: Ancient Near Eastern bricks were 10 to 24 inches long and 6 to 13½ inches wide.
Or perhaps “draw.”
verses.commentary:
4:1 "son of man" See note at Ezek. 2:1.

YHWH commands the prophet to do several dramatic acts of judgment which depict the fall
of Jerusalem. Because of Ezek. 3:25, these dramatic acts were probably performed in front of his house, in
public view.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SON OF MAN

▣ "Get yourself a brick" BDB 527 says that this refers to a tile, not a brick, but
the lexicon KB 518 says it was a sun-baked brick (larger in size than modern bricks), probably
of white clay. It is uncertain if it was soft clay, which was normally used for writing, or baked
clay with an outline of the city scratched into it.

- get a brick, Ezek. 4:1, BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERATIVE

- set it before you

- inscribe (outline of the city of Jerusalem) on it

- build siege wall, ramps, camps around the brick

- place battering rams (i.e. another Qal IMPERATIVE)

- get an iron plate, Ezek. 4:3, BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERATIVE
(used as a divider)

- lie on your side, Ezek. 4:4, BDB 1011, KB 1486, Qal IMPERATIVE

- take (food items), BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERATIVE

- take (sharp sword and cut off hair and beard), Ezek. 5:1, BDB 542, KB 534, Qal
IMPERATIVE

The entire context (i.e. chaps. 4-5 is a literary unit) is one sustained dramatic act foreshadowing
the siege and fall of Jerusalem.

These dramatic prophetic acts of Ezekiel occurred exactly four years before the siege of Jerusalem by
Neo-Babylon, which resulted in the total destruction of the city (i.e. 586 B.C.). Chapters 4 and 5 contain a series
of silent, dramatic acts related to God's enforced silence of Ezek. 3:26.

verses.zh: 又围困这城，造台筑垒，安营攻击，在四围安设撞锤攻城，
verses.en: Lay siege to it! Build siege works against it. Erect a siege ramp[NOTE:1] against it! Post soldiers outside it[NOTE:2] and station battering rams around it.
notes: Or “a barricade.”
Heb “set camps against it.”
verses.commentary:
4:2 "siege-wall" This (BDB 189, KB 220) was a series of siege towers that were built to put the archers of the
invaders on level with the ramparts of the city (cf. 2 Kgs. 25:1; Jer. 52:4; Ezek. 4:2; 17:17; 21:27; 26:8).

▣ "raise up a ramp" This was an earthen ramp (BDB 700, KB 757, cf. 2 Sam. 20:15; Jer. 32:24; 33:4) where
the ramming instruments (BDB 503, cf. Ezek. 4:2; 21:27) could be brought against the walls of the city (e.g.
the Roman ramp at Masada).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SIEGE MOUNDS

verses.zh: 又要拿个铁鏊，放在你和城的中间，作为铁墙。你要对面攻击这城，使城被困；这样，好作以色列家的预兆。
verses.en: Then for your part take an iron frying pan[NOTE:1] and set it up as an iron wall between you and the city. Set your face toward it. It is to be under siege; you are to besiege it. This is a sign[NOTE:2] for the house of Israel.
notes: Or “a griddle,” that is, some sort of plate for cooking.
That is, a symbolic object lesson.
verses.commentary:
4:3 "an iron plate" This (BDB 290) is used in Lev. 2:5; 6:21 for a small, concave plate for the baking
of bread. In context it seems to relate to God setting His face against His own people and not hearing their
cries for help (i.e. His prophet/priest is silent, cf. Ezek. 3:25-27).

▣ "this is a sign to the house of Israel" Signs (BDB 16) were God's way to show His people that
He was in control of history. Ezekiel uses this phrase often (cf. Ezek. 4:3; 12:6,11; 24:24). Ezekiel's
God-given signs were a dramatic way to communicate with the exiled community. It is uncertain if all of
these signs were literally acted out or were literary in nature. The truth and trustworthiness of God's
message remains the same either way. One wonders how Ezek. 4:8 could be literal or related to Ezek. 3:25.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SIGN (OT)

verses.zh: 你要向左侧卧，承当以色列家的罪孽；要按你向左侧卧的日数，担当他们的罪孽。
verses.en: “Also for your part lie on your left side and place the iniquity[NOTE:1] of the house of Israel on it. For the number of days you lie on your side you will bear their iniquity.
notes: Or “punishment” (also in vv. 5, 6).
verses.commentary:
4:4 God commands the prophet to lie (BDB 1011, KB 1486, Qal IMPERATIVE) on his left
side to bear (BDB 669, KB 724, lit. "to carry," Qal IMPERFECT) the sin of Israel. Apparently
this is a function of the priesthood (cf. Num. 18:1). The VERB implies the carrying away of sin,
like the scapegoat in the ceremony of Leviticus 16, the Day of Atonement. However, Ezekiel's actions do not
cause God to spare Jerusalem, but judge it (cf. Ezek. 4:7). Ezekiel's acts show the extent of the people's
rebellion (i.e. longevity).

verses.zh: 因为我已将他们作孽的年数定为你向左侧卧的日数，就是三百九十日，你要这样担当以色列家的罪孽。
verses.en: I have determined that the number of the years of their iniquity are to be the number of days[NOTE:1] for you—390 days.[NOTE:2] So bear the iniquity of the house of Israel.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “I have assigned for you that the years of their iniquity be the number of days.” Num 14:33-34 is an example of the reverse, where the days were converted into years, the number of days spying out the land becoming the number of years of the wilderness wanderings.

The LXX reads “190 days.” sn The significance of the number 390 is not clear. The best explanation is that “days” are used figuratively for years and the number refers to the years of the sinfulness of Israel during the period of the First Temple. Some understand the number to refer to the length of the division of the northern and southern kingdoms down to the fall of Jerusalem (931-586 b.c.), but this adds up to only 345 years.
Or “When you have carried the iniquity of the house of Israel,” and continuing on to the next verse.
verses.commentary:
4:5 "three hundred and ninety days" Ezekiel is told to lie on his side to show the sin of both Israel
(Ezek. 4:4-5) and Judah (Ezek. 4:6). It is obvious here that "the house of Israel" means the Northern
Ten Tribes only.

There has been much difficulty concerning "390 days." The Septuagint has "190 days" and this may
be closer to the original number because the difference in time between Ezek. 1:2 and 8:1 is only 14 months,
which seems not to leave enough time for 430 days of silent witness (i.e. 390 for Israel and 40 for Judah).

It is possible that the combined numbers (i.e. 390 + 40) equals Israel's time in Egypt plus
the wilderness wanderings (cf. Gen. 15:13; Exod. 12:40; Acts 7:6; Gal. 3:17). Therefore, it might be a way of
referring to the beginning of Israel as a people (i.e. Abraham - Moses). If so, it symbolized that they had
always been a sinful, rebellious, stiff-necked people (cf. Ezek. 2:3-4,7,8).

We as moderns must remember that the ancients used certain numbers in symbolic ways. Often
these are round numbers (cf. John J. Davis, Biblical Numerology).

verses.zh: 再者，你满了这些日子，还要向右侧卧，担当犹大家的罪孽。我给你定规侧卧四十日，一日顶一年。
verses.en: “When you have completed these days, then lie down a second time, but on your right side, and bear the iniquity of the house of Judah 40 days[NOTE:1]—I have assigned one day for each year.
notes: The number 40 may refer in general to the period of Judah’s exile, indicating the number of years Israel was punished in the wilderness. In this case, however, one would need to translate, “you will bear the punishment of the house of Judah.”
verses.commentary:
4:6 "forty days" The number forty in the Bible is often a long period of indefinite time. Why this different number
applies to Judah is uncertain.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #7

verses.zh: 你要露出膀臂，面向被困的耶路撒冷，说预言攻击这城。
verses.en: You must turn your face toward the siege of Jerusalem with your arm bared and prophesy against it.
verses.commentary:
4:7 "with your arm bared" This was imagery for God's effective action against Jerusalem.

God's arm/hand can be for good or woe.

- positive, Exod. 6:6; 15:16; Deut. 4:34; 5:15; 7:19; 2 Chr. 32:8; Ps. 98:1; Isa. 52:10; Jer. 32:17-18

- negative, Jer. 6:12; 21:5; 27:5-6; Ezek. 20:33-34; 30:24-25

verses.zh: 我用绳索捆绑你，使你不能辗转，直等你满了困城的日子。
verses.en: Look here: I will tie you up with ropes, so you cannot turn from one side to the other until you complete the days of your siege.[NOTE:1]
notes: The action surely refers to a series of daily acts rather than to a continuous period.
verses.commentary:
4:8 "I will put ropes on you" This same imagery is used in Ezek. 3:25. God directs the prophet's words
and actions to communicate His message to His people.

It seems from Ezek. 3:25 that the prophet was limited to his home. The elders had to go there
to see him (cf. Ezek. 8:1; 14:1; 20:1). He was also allowed to communicate either by a message or a dramatic
act only if God directed him.

verses.zh: 你要取小麦、大麦、豆子、红豆、小米、粗麦，装在一个器皿中，用以为自己做饼；要按你侧卧的三百九十日吃这饼。
verses.en: “As for you, take wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt,[NOTE:1] put them in a single container, and make food[NOTE:2] from them for yourself. For the same number of days that you lie on your side—390 days[NOTE:3]—you will eat it.
notes: Wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt. All these foods were common in Mesopotamia where Ezekiel was exiled.
Heb “bread.”
The LXX reads: “190 days.”
verses.commentary:
4:9-17 The dramatic action of Ezekiel lying on his side was only part of the symbolism; what he ate
and drank and how much he ate and drank also had significance (cf. Ezek. 4:16-17). The siege would cause
famine in Jerusalem.

- A food shortage required that the people eat a combination of grains, some of which were not
normally eaten.

- It meant less water per day.

- There would be no wood or oil to cook with. Animal dung would be the only source of fuel

Cow dung was and still is (i.e. India) often used as fuel.

verses.zh: 你所吃的要按分两吃，每日二十舍客勒，按时而吃。
verses.en: The food you eat will be eight ounces[NOTE:1] a day by weight; you must eat it at fixed times.[NOTE:2]
notes: Eight ounces (Heb “twenty shekels”). The standards for weighing money varied considerably in the ancient Near East, but the generally accepted weight for the shekel is 11.5 grams (0.4 ounce). This makes the weight of grain about 230 grams here (8 ounces).
Heb “from time to time.”
verses.commentary:
4:10 "twenty shekels a day by weight" This would equal about 8-10 ounces of bread. This amount is
too small for a healthy diet.

▣ "from time to time" This is a Hebrew idiom which means at a set time each day (cf. Ezek. 4:11;
1 Chr. 9:25).

verses.zh: 你喝水也要按制子，每日喝一欣六分之一，按时而喝。
verses.en: And you must drink water by measure, a pint and a half;[NOTE:1] you must drink it at fixed times.
notes: A pint and a half [Heb “one-sixth of a hin”]. One-sixth of a hin was a quantity of liquid equal to about 1.3 pints or 0.6 liters.
verses.commentary:
4:11 "a sixth part of a hin by measure" This would be a little under a pint, according to rabbinical
commentators. Ezekiel would lose weight and strength on this diet, which mimicked a siege situation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANE WEIGHTS AND VOLUMES (Metrology)

verses.zh: 你吃这饼像吃大麦饼一样，要用人粪在众人眼前烧烤。」
verses.en: And you must eat the food as you would a barley cake. You must bake it in front of them over a fire made with dried human excrement.”[NOTE:1]
notes: Human waste was to remain outside the camp of the Israelites according to Deut 23:12-14.

verses.zh: 耶和华说：「以色列人在我所赶他们到的各国中，也必这样吃不洁净的食物。」
verses.en: And the Lord said, “This is how the people of Israel will eat their unclean food among the nations[NOTE:1] where I will banish them.”
notes: Unclean food among the nations. Lands outside of Israel were considered unclean (Josh 22:19; Amos 7:17).
verses.commentary:
4:13 Using dung as a cooking fuel would make the inhabitants of Jerusalem ceremonially unclean. It
would be a symbol of the Levitically unclean food they would be forced to eat as exiles in a foreign land
(cf. Dan. 1:8; Hosea 9:3-4).

▣ "I shall banish them" This VERB (BDB 623, KB 673, Hiphil IMPERFECT)
describes YHWH's sending the covenant people out of the Promised Land (cf. Jer. 8:3; 16:15; 24:9; 27:10,15). However,
if they repent, YHWH will restore them (cf. Deut. 30:1,4; Jer. 23:3,8; 29:14; 32:37; 46:28).

Ezekiel presents YHWH's message of the destruction and exile of Jerusalem until it happens and
then his message changes to one of a divine restoration (cf. chaps. 33-48).

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

verses.zh: 我说：「哎！主耶和华啊，我素来未曾被玷污，从幼年到如今没有吃过自死的，或被野兽撕裂的，那可憎的肉也未曾入我的口。」
verses.en: And I said, “Ah, Sovereign Lord, I have never been ceremonially defiled before. I have never eaten a carcass or an animal torn by wild beasts; from my youth up, unclean meat[NOTE:1] has never entered my mouth.”
notes: The Hebrew term refers to sacrificial meat not eaten by the appropriate time (Lev 7:18; 19:7).
verses.commentary:
4:14 "I have never eaten what died of itself or was torn by beasts" This relates to Ezekiel's squeamishness
("I have never been defiled," BDB 379, KB 375, Pual PARTICIPLE) about the uncleanness involved
in this symbolic act. The human dung was the primary issue (cf. Ezek. 4:12), but he expands his affirmation of
his faithfulness to the Mosaic Law in Ezek. 4:14. He would be referring to animals that had not been properly
killed and bled (cf. Exod. 22:31; Lev. 17:11-16; Deut. 12:16). God responds to the prophet's squeamishness and
allows cow dung (BDB 861, only here in the OT) to be substituted for fuel in Ezek. 4:15.

The MT has "nephesh," translated "I." See notes online at Gen. 35:18
and Lev. 17:11.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

verses.zh: 于是他对我说：「看哪，我给你牛粪代替人粪，你要将你的饼烤在其上。」
verses.en: So he said to me, “All right then, I will substitute cow’s manure instead of human excrement. You will cook your food over it.”

verses.zh: 他又对我说：「人子啊，我必在耶路撒冷折断他们的杖，就是断绝他们的粮。他们吃饼要按分两，忧虑而吃；喝水也要按制子，惊惶而喝；
verses.en: Then he said to me, “Son of man, I am about to remove the bread supply[NOTE:1] in Jerusalem.[NOTE:2] They will eat their bread ration anxiously, and they will drink their water ration in terror
notes: Heb, “break the staff of bread.” The bread supply is compared to a staff that one uses for support.
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
verses.commentary:
4:16 "the staff of bread" This unusual imagery uses "staff" in the sense of supply (cf. Lev. 26:26;
Ps. 105:16; Isa. 3:1; Ezek. 4:16-17; 5:16; 14:13).

verses.zh: 使他们缺粮缺水，彼此惊惶，因自己的罪孽消灭。」
verses.en: because they will lack bread and water. Each one will be terrified, and they will rot for their iniquity.[NOTE:1]
notes: Or “in their punishment.” Ezek 4:16-17 alludes to Lev 26:26, 39. The phrase “in/for [a person’s] iniquity” occurs fourteen times in Ezekiel: here, 3:18, 19; 7:13, 16; 18:17, 18, 19, 20; 24:23; 33:6, 8, 9; 39:23. The Hebrew word for “iniquity” may also mean the “punishment for iniquity.”
verses.commentary:
4:17 "waste away in their iniquity" The VERB (BDB 596, KB 628, Niphal
PERFECT with waw) means

- fester, Ps. 38:5

- rot, Zech. 14:12 (three times)

- wear away or dissolve, Isa. 34:4

It is used three times in Ezekiel describing YHWH's judgment on His people (cf. Ezek. 4:17; 24:23;
33:10). The choice of this term by Ezekiel may go back to Lev. 26:39, where it is used twice. Ezekiel, as a
trained priest, drew much of his vocabulary from Leviticus.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible.
Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing
is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY
